claim: Vibrio cholerae biofilms display disordered cores decorated with radial features extending to the rims.
source: This strain (denoted WT in the present work) produces biofilms that have disordered cores decorated with radial features extending to the rims (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1A showing the biofilm morphology.

claim: Biofilm surface morphology changes with increasing agar concentration, with spacing between peripheral radial features reduced and amplitudes becoming more homogeneous.
source: Indeed, biofilm surface morphology changes with increasing agar concentration: the spacing between the peripheral, radial features is reduced and their amplitudes become more homogeneous (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A biofilm growing at an air–liquid interface exhibits no surface features.
source: Indeed, a biofilm growing at an air–liquid interface, not limited or compressed by a substrate, exhibits no surface features (Video 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by video evidence showing biofilm growth at air-liquid interface.

claim: Biofilms possess finite adhesion strength of approximately 5 mJ/m².
source: Biofilms possess finite adhesion strength (~ 5 mJ/m2), which is the same order of magnitude as the deformation energy of the soft substrate (Yan et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with a specific measurement value and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A large localized blister forms at the collision front where mechanical stress is most concentrated when two biofilms collide.
source: Indeed, a large localized blister formed at the collision front where mechanical stress is most concentrated (Figure 1C; Video 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Video 2.

claim: Wrinkling and delamination occur at the biofilm periphery with no preceding localized cell death.
source: However, in the biofilm periphery, which is the region of focus of the current study, wrinkling and delamination occur with no preceding localized cell death (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: During cell proliferation, radial compressive stress is partially relieved by new biomass extending the biofilm boundary.
source: During cell proliferation, radial compressive stress is partially relieved by new biomass extending the biofilm boundary (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citation to previous theoretical work.

claim: In the tangential direction, compressive stress becomes concentrated because there is no analogous relaxation mechanism.
source: By contrast, in the tangential direction, compressive stress becomes concentrated because there is no analogous relaxation mechanism.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on logical inference from the mechanical model.

claim: The wrinkling wavelength is determined exclusively by the thickness and mechanical properties of the relevant materials for a film–substrate system subject to compressive stress.
source: Mechanical instability theory predicts that, for a film–substrate system that is subject to compressive stress, the wrinkling wavelength is determined exclusively by the thickness and mechanical properties of the relevant materials (Huang et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citation to established mechanical instability theory.

claim: There is a linear relationship between the number of wrinkles or blisters N and radial distance r from the biofilm center.
source: We found a linear relationship between N and r (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The slope of the N versus r relationship has a geometrical origin: N = (2π/λ)r where λ is the inherent wavelength of the system.
source: The slope has a geometrical origin: N = (2π/λ)r in which λ is the inherent wavelength of the system irrespective of the time in the developmental process or the location in the overall pattern (except at the biofilm core).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on geometric analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Radial wrinkles or blisters must bifurcate to maintain constant spacing as r increases.
source: A constant wavelength λ also means that radial wrinkles or blisters must bifurcate to maintain constant spacing as r increases, and indeed, we observed this to be the case (Figure 2A, inset).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 2A inset.

claim: The biofilm shear modulus Gf varies minimally over a wide range of agar concentrations.
source: Gf varies minimally over a wide range of agar concentrations, whereas Gs varies by almost three orders of magnitude for agar concentrations from 0.4% to 3% (Supplementary file 1 Table S1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental measurements in Supplementary file 1 Table S1.

claim: The substrate shear modulus Gs varies by almost three orders of magnitude for agar concentrations from 0.4% to 3%.
source: Gf varies minimally over a wide range of agar concentrations, whereas Gs varies by almost three orders of magnitude for agar concentrations from 0.4% to 3% (Supplementary file 1 Table S1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental measurements in Supplementary file 1 Table S1.

claim: Plotting λ/h versus Gf/Gs on a log-log scale reveals the characteristic scaling power law of 1/3.
source: Plotting λ/h versus Gf/Gs on a log-log scale (Figure 2B) reveals the characteristic scaling power law of 1/3, indicating the applicability of mechanical instability theory to biofilm morphogenesis.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Bilayer theory predicts that if Gf/Gs < 1.3, the substrate is too stiff for the flat-to-wrinkling transition to occur.
source: Bilayer theory predicts that, if Gf/Gs < 1.3, the substrate is too stiff for the flat-to-wrinkling transition to occur (Wang and Zhao, 2015).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citation to established theory.

claim: Wrinkling occurs in biofilm experiments for Gf/Gs well below 1.3, corresponding to agar concentrations ≥ 0.7%.
source: However, wrinkling occurs in our experiments for Gf/Gs well below 1.3, corresponding to agar concentrations ≥ 0.7%.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on experimental observations.

claim: A third soft, intermediate layer exists between the growing biofilm and the non-growing substrate.
source: To reconcile this discrepancy, we considered that a third soft, intermediate layer could exist between the growing biofilm and the non-growing substrate, which has been shown to allow wrinkling behavior even at low Gf/Gs ratios (Lejeune et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citation to previous work on trilayer systems.

claim: A residual layer remains on the substrate after biofilm peeling with a thickness hr.
source: After peeling, a residual layer remained on the substrate with a thickness hr (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The residual layer consists primarily of matrix polysaccharide.
source: Our preliminary analysis suggests that this layer consists primarily of matrix polysaccharide (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: The corrected biofilm thickness hf is obtained as hf = h – hr.
source: Thus, the corrected biofilm thickness hf was obtained as hf = h – hr.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on the measurement methodology.

claim: With a soft intermediate layer, the wrinkling pattern persists even when the substrate becomes stiffer than the biofilm (Gs > Gf).
source: Qualitatively, with a soft intermediate layer, the wrinkling pattern persists even when the substrate becomes stiffer than the biofilm (Gs > Gf).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on the trilayer model predictions.

claim: In the trilayer model, the soft interfacial layer assumes the major share of the deformation, effectively reducing the substrate stiffness.
source: Unlike the bilayer model, in which the substrate is deformed by the wrinkling film, in the trilayer model, the soft interfacial layer assumes the major share of the deformation, effectively reducing the substrate stiffness (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 4) (Lejeune et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by modeling results and citation.

claim: An intermediate layer stiffness of Gr = 0.1Gf allows the trilayer model to best fit experimental data over all conditions.
source: An intermediate layer stiffness of Gr = 0.1Gf allows the trilayer model to best fit our experimental data over all conditions.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on fitting the trilayer model to experimental data.

claim: Whether and when a film–substrate system undergoes delamination is controlled by a competition between the adhesion energy between layers, Γ, and the elastic energy in the substrate.
source: Whether and when a film–substrate system undergoes delamination is controlled by a competition between the adhesion energy between layers, Γ , and the elastic energy in the substrate.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on established mechanical theory.

claim: The biofilm–agar interfacial adhesion energy Γ is approximately 5–10 mJ/m².
source: We recently measured the biofilm–agar interfacial adhesion energy Γ ~ 5–10 mJ/m2 (Yan et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citation to previous measurement work.

claim: Γ* is in the order of 0.01–1 in the biofilm system, making delamination highly likely to occur during biofilm growth.
source: Hence, Γ* is in the order of 0.01–1 in the current system, making delamination highly likely to occur during biofilm growth.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on calculation from measured parameters.

claim: In the context of the trilayer model, delamination takes place at the weakest interface, which is between the biofilm and the residual layer.
source: In the context of the trilayer model, delamination takes place at the weakest interface, which is between the biofilm and the residual layer.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on the trilayer model interpretation.

claim: Radial wrinkles developed into blisters when growth proceeded beyond approximately 36 hr.
source: Radial wrinkles developed into blisters when growth proceeded beyond ~ 36 hr.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on experimental observations.

claim: At low agar concentrations, large amplitude blisters emerged among small amplitude wrinkles.
source: At low agar concentrations, large amplitude blisters emerged among small amplitude wrinkles (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At higher agar concentrations, additional wrinkles developed into blisters, although with amplitudes smaller than those on low concentration agar substrates.
source: At higher agar concentrations, additional wrinkles developed into blisters, although with amplitudes smaller than those on low concentration agar substrates.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on experimental observations.

claim: At low agar concentration (0.6%), only a small fraction of wrinkles were detached from the substrate in the form of blisters.
source: At low agar concentration (i.e., 0.6%), only a small fraction of wrinkles were detached from the substrate in the form of blisters (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: At high agar concentration (1.0%), nearly all wrinkles had developed into blisters.
source: By contrast, at high agar concentration (i.e. 1.0%), nearly all wrinkles had developed into blisters.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on experimental observations.

claim: Voids were clearly present underneath the blisters, which were presumably filled with liquid.
source: In the cross-sectional images, voids were clearly present underneath the blisters, which were presumably filled with liquid (Wilking et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by cross-sectional imaging and citation.

claim: There is a positive correlation between the percentage of wrinkles that converted to blisters at the biofilm edge and the substrate agar concentration.
source: Figure 3D quantifies the positive correlation between the percentage of wrinkles that converted to blisters at the biofilm edge and the substrate agar concentration.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: On stiff substrates, Γ* is small, so delamination is favored over wrinkling.
source: On stiff substrates, Γ* is small, so delamination is favored over wrinkling.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on the mechanical model interpretation.

claim: On soft substrates, Γ* is large, so blisters form only infrequently while the majority of the biofilm remains attached to the substrate.
source: On soft substrates, Γ* is large, so blisters form only infrequently while the majority of the biofilm remains attached to the substrate.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on the mechanical model interpretation.

claim: The locations of blisters on soft substrates are defined by surface defects that trigger local delamination.
source: We hypothesized that the locations of blisters on soft substrates are defined by surface defects that trigger local delamination.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a hypothesis based on observations.

claim: Predefined surface imperfections dictated the exact locations at which blisters formed as the biofilm expanded on soft substrates.
source: Indeed, these imperfections dictated the exact locations at which blisters formed as the biofilm expanded.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on experimental observations with patterned substrates.

claim: On stiff substrates, delamination occurred along the entire biofilm rim, irrespective of the predefined surface imperfections.
source: By contrast, on stiff substrates, delamination occurred along the entire biofilm rim, irrespective of the predefined surface imperfections (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The width of each biofilm blister decreased while its height increased over time until the final width of the blister reached twice that of the thickness of the biofilm.
source: The width of each biofilm blister decreased while its height increased over time until the final width of the blister reached twice that of the thickness of the biofilm (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental tracking data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: After the blister width reaches twice the biofilm thickness, blisters continue to develop only in height.
source: Subsequently, blisters continue to develop only in height.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on experimental observations.

claim: Large blisters suppress nearby wrinkles from delaminating.
source: Moreover, large blisters suppress nearby wrinkles from delaminating (Figure 4B), presumably because the biofilm and the substrate can slide relative to one another such that a blister captures nearby compressed biofilm material, and in so doing, releases compressive stress in the vicinity.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Neighboring blisters tend to merge during late stages of biofilm development (>48 hr).
source: Neighboring blisters tend to merge during late stages of biofilm development (>48 hr), forming single dark features in the transmission images (Figure 4C (top) and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental imaging data.

claim: Cross-sectional images reveal that head-to-head contact occurred between neighboring blisters.
source: Indeed, cross-sectional images reveal that head-to-head contact occurred (Figure 4C (bottom)).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by cross-sectional imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The biofilm–liquid interface energy γfl is approximately 49 mJ/m².
source: They are: biofilm blister–liquid underneath, γfl ~ 49 mJ/m2; biofilm blister–air above, γfa ~ 30 mJ/m2; and the energy needed to separate the biofilm from the residual layer underneath, Γ ~ 5 mJ/m2 (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The biofilm–air interface energy γfa is approximately 30 mJ/m².
source: They are: biofilm blister–liquid underneath, γfl ~ 49 mJ/m2; biofilm blister–air above, γfa ~ 30 mJ/m2; and the energy needed to separate the biofilm from the residual layer underneath, Γ ~ 5 mJ/m2 (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The energy needed to separate the biofilm from the residual layer is approximately 5 mJ/m².
source: They are: biofilm blister–liquid underneath, γfl ~ 49 mJ/m2; biofilm blister–air above, γfa ~ 30 mJ/m2; and the energy needed to separate the biofilm from the residual layer underneath, Γ ~ 5 mJ/m2 (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The energy hierarchy determines the sequence through which interfaces are generated or annihilated.
source: This energy hierarchy determines the sequence through which interfaces are generated or annihilated (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on the measured interfacial energies.

claim: Compressive stress leads to delamination of the biofilm from the residual layer, forming a local blister.
source: First, compressive stress leads to delamination of the biofilm from the residual layer, forming a local blister.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on the mechanomorphogenesis model.

claim: To eliminate the high-energy interface between the blister and the liquid underneath, the two sides of the inner face of the blister come into contact with each other as the blister grows.
source: To eliminate this high-energy interface, the two sides of the inner face of the blister come into contact with each other as the blister grows.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on the interfacial energy model.

claim: Electron microscopy imaging of the cross-section of a blister shows that the two sides of the inner face contact each other.
source: Indeed, electron microscopy imaging of the cross-section of a blister shows this to be the case (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by SEM imaging data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: After internal contact occurs, the blister can only develop in the vertical direction.
source: After internal contact occurs, the blister can only develop in the vertical direction.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on geometric constraints.

claim: Subsequent merging of neighboring blisters eliminates biofilm–air interfaces, lowering the free energy of the entire system.
source: Subsequent merging of neighboring blisters (Figure 4C) eliminates biofilm–air interfaces, and in so doing, lowers the free energy of the entire system.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on interfacial energy considerations.

claim: Cells in blisters are less susceptible to the lethal effects of antibiotics that diffuse in from the substrate than are cells residing in the base of the biofilm.
source: An added benefit to the bacteria stems from these blister dynamics: cells in blisters are less susceptible to the lethal effects of antibiotics that diffuse in from the substrate than are cells residing in the base of the biofilm, presumably because cells in blisters are located further away from the antibiotic source (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The Δbap1ΔrbmC biofilm exhibits a star-shaped morphology with flat regions between the facets of the stars when formed on soft agar substrates.
source: Rather than forming isolated blisters, when formed on soft agar substrates, the Δbap1ΔrbmC biofilm exhibits a star-shaped morphology with flat regions between the facets of the stars (Figure 5A (top)) (Yan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental imaging data in Figure 5A and citation.

claim: The cross-section of a single facet in the Δbap1ΔrbmC biofilm shows that it consists of a group of congregated blisters.
source: The cross-section of a single facet shows that it consists of a group of congregated blisters (Figure 5A (bottom)).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by cross-sectional imaging data in Figure 5A.

claim: In the Δbap1ΔrbmC mutant, only the external surfaces of neighboring blisters are in contact with one another, leaving the internal spaces under each blister intact.
source: Curiously, in contrast to the WT blisters, in the mutant, only the external surfaces of neighboring blisters are in contact with one another, leaving the internal spaces under each blister intact.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on experimental observations.

claim: The adhesion energy Γ between the Δbap1ΔrbmC biofilm and the substrate is below the detection limit.
source: The adhesion energy Γ between the Δbap1ΔrbmC biofilm and the substrate is below the detection limit, meaning that delamination occurs more easily in the Δbap1ΔrbmC biofilm than in the WT biofilm.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the Δbap1ΔrbmC mutant, γfl approaches zero whereas γfa is large, consistent with the hydrophilicity of the Δbap1ΔrbmC biofilm.
source: Second, the relative order of interfacial energies changes in the mutant: γfl approaches zero whereas γfa is large, consistent with the hydrophilicity of the Δbap1ΔrbmC biofilm (Hollenbeck et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental measurements and citation.

claim: Δbap1ΔrbmC biofilm blisters emerge directly from the expanding flat film, skipping the wrinkling state.
source: Indeed, Δbap1ΔrbmC biofilm blisters emerge directly from the expanding flat film, skipping the wrinkling state (Video 6).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by video evidence.

claim: In the Δbap1ΔrbmC mutant, neighboring blisters prefer to collapse against each other, which eliminates the high-energy interface between the biofilm and the air.
source: Instead of annihilating biofilm–liquid interfaces inside of the blisters, in the mutant, neighboring blisters prefer to collapse against each other, which eliminates the high-energy interface between the biofilm and the air.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on the altered interfacial energy hierarchy.

claim: During the development of the Δbap1ΔrbmC mutant biofilm, newly emergent blisters move towards, and ultimately join, existing blister groups.
source: Indeed, during the development of the mutant biofilm, newly emergent blisters move towards, and ultimately join, existing blister groups (Figure 5E; Video 6).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental imaging data in Figure 5E and Video 6.

claim: The triangular shape of each facet in the Δbap1ΔrbmC biofilm is a consequence of the merging of multiple blisters, whose ages and radial lengths decrease from the center to the edge of the aggregate.
source: The triangular shape of each facet in the Δbap1ΔrbmC biofilm is therefore a consequence of the merging of multiple blisters, whose ages and radial lengths decrease from the center to the edge of the aggregate.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on analysis of blister dynamics.

claim: For a biofilm growing on soft agar (0.4%), there is a sharp increase in acircularity α at tc, the time at which the 3D surface morphology forms at the edge.
source: For a biofilm growing on soft agar (0.4%, Figure 6A), there is a sharp increase in α at tc, the time at which the 3D surface morphology forms at the edge (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutant biofilms lacking the matrix structural polysaccharide (ΔvpsL) have no surface features and α remains close to 1.
source: To show that blisters are required for contour undulations, we tracked α for mutant biofilms lacking the matrix structural polysaccharide (ΔvpsL) (Figure 4—figure supplement 3; Hammer and Bassler, 2003) or lacking matrix structural proteins (ΔrbmAΔbap1ΔrbmC) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C; Berk et al., 2012; Yan et al., 2017). In both cases, the biofilm has no surface features and α remains close to 1 (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data in Figure 6A and citations.

claim: Mutant biofilms lacking matrix structural proteins (ΔrbmAΔbap1ΔrbmC) have no surface features and α remains close to 1.
source: To show that blisters are required for contour undulations, we tracked α for mutant biofilms lacking the matrix structural polysaccharide (ΔvpsL) (Figure 4—figure supplement 3; Hammer and Bassler, 2003) or lacking matrix structural proteins (ΔrbmAΔbap1ΔrbmC) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C; Berk et al., 2012; Yan et al., 2017). In both cases, the biofilm has no surface features and α remains close to 1 (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data in Figure 6A and citations.

claim: The indentations along the biofilm contours always correspond to the locations of large blisters.
source: Visually, the indentations along the contours always correspond to the locations of large blisters.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on visual analysis of biofilm images.

claim: Both local curvature κ and expansion velocity Vf are negatively correlated with the positions of blisters.
source: To quantify this finding, we measured the local curvature κ and expansion velocity Vf along the biofilm periphery (Figure 6B,C, Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2). Both κ and Vf are negatively correlated with the positions of blisters.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6B,C and supplements.

claim: The emergence of a blister creates an extra dimension into which newly produced biomass can be distributed, which causes local slowing in Vf.
source: The emergence of a blister creates an extra dimension into which newly produced biomass can be distributed, which causes local slowing in Vf, thus establishing the correlation between blister locations and negative local curvature.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on analysis of blister formation effects.

claim: WT biofilms grown on stiff agar (>1.0%) remain nearly circular because they possess regularly and closely spaced blisters.
source: This explanation for the formation of the biofilm petal shapes suggests that contour undulations require non-homogeneous blister distribution along the biofilm rim and indeed, WT biofilms that are grown on stiff agar (>1.0%) remain nearly circular because they possess regularly and closely spaced blisters (Figure 6A, blue line).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data in Figure 6A.

claim: The number and positions of the petals can be controlled by specifying the positions of the blisters using patterned substrates.
source: As additional evidence for the connection between blister formation and boundary undulation, we show that we can control the number and positions of the petals by specifying the positions of the blisters using patterned substrates (Figure 3, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data in Figure 3 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mechanical instabilities, including wrinkling and delamination, underlie biofilm morphogenesis.
source: We show here that mechanical instabilities, including wrinkling and delamination, underlie biofilm morphogenesis.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a main conclusion of the study.

claim: Differences in interfacial energies drive mechanomorphogenesis by dictating the creation or annihilation of new or existing interfaces.
source: Moreover, differences in interfacial energies drive mechanomorphogenesis by dictating the creation or annihilation of new or existing interfaces.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a main conclusion of the study.

claim: Feedback between mechanomorphogenesis and biofilm expansion shapes the overall biofilm contour.
source: Finally, feedback between mechanomorphogenesis and biofilm expansion shapes the overall biofilm contour.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The morphogenesis principles discovered in bacterial biofilms, which rely on mechanical instabilities and interfacial energies, should be generally applicable to morphogenesis processes in tissues in higher organisms.
source: The morphogenesis principles that we discover in bacterial biofilms, which rely on mechanical instabilities and interfacial energies, should be generally applicable to morphogenesis processes in tissues in higher organisms.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a main conclusion and speculation about broader applicability.

claim: Localized cell death can be viewed as a source of surface defects that functions to trigger delaminations.
source: In fact, in light of our mechanomorphogenesis model, localized cell death can be viewed as a source of surface defects that functions to trigger delaminations, similar to the defined surface imperfections that drive delaminations shown in Figure 3E.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an interpretation of previous findings in light of the current model.

claim: The mechanical principles uncovered in V. cholerae could also drive the morphological transitions in P. aeruginosa biofilms.
source: We suggest that the mechanical principles uncovered here could also drive the morphological transitions in P. aeruginosa biofilms.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a suggestion for broader applicability.

claim: The WT P. aeruginosa biofilm pattern occurs because cells at the biofilm center display upregulated matrix production, whereas cells located at the periphery are downregulated for matrix production.
source: The WT P. aeruginosa biofilm pattern occurs because cells at the biofilm center display upregulated matrix production (Madsen et al., 2015), whereas cells located at the periphery are downregulated for matrix production.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In the case of the Δphz mutant, all of the cells overproduce extracellular polysaccharides.
source: In the case of the Δphz mutant, all of the cells overproduce extracellular polysaccharides (Madsen et al., 2015), so we speculate that the Δphz P. aeruginosa mutant forms peripheral radial wrinkles and subsequently delaminations because of the same mechanical instability described here in V. cholerae.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Gene regulation and spatially differentiated cell physiology can be coupled to mechanical instability to promote biofilm surface morphologies.
source: These examples illustrate how gene regulation and spatially differentiated cell physiology can be coupled to mechanical instability to promote biofilm surface morphologies.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a conclusion about the interplay between biology and mechanics.

claim: The thin intermediate residual layer is required to explain the wrinkling instability in biofilms.
source: For example, the thin intermediate residual layer that we discovered here is not accurately considered in biofilm simulations, but is required to explain the wrinkling instability in biofilms (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by modeling results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Interfacial energies play a predominant role in driving the morphologies of biological materials that possess soft layers.
source: In addition, interfacial energies play a predominant role in driving the morphologies of biological materials that possess soft layers, whereas their roles are minor in classical mechanical systems (Qi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The cerebellum possesses a thin, soft layer of Purkinje cells that is sandwiched between the rapidly growing external granular layer and the slow-growing internal granular layer.
source: The cerebellum possesses a thin, soft layer of Purkinje cells that is sandwiched between the rapidly growing external granular layer and the slow-growing internal granular layer (Lejeune et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Through wrinkling instabilities, the cerebellum develops finely spaced parallel grooves called folia.
source: Through wrinkling instabilities, the cerebellum develops finely spaced parallel grooves called folia.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on established knowledge about cerebellum development.

claim: The hard-soft-hard geometry and the associated wrinkling instabilities in the cerebellum directly mirror the configuration discovered in V. cholerae biofilms.
source: This hard-soft-hard geometry and the associated wrinkling instabilities directly mirror the configuration that we discovered in V. cholerae biofilms.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a comparison between biofilm and cerebellum morphogenesis.

claim: Exploiting mechanical principles to drive key morphogenic events is ancient: it occurs in bacteria, and evolution has reused prokaryotic processes and principles in eukaryotes.
source: Hence, our work suggests that exploiting mechanical principles to drive key morphogenic events is ancient: it occurs in bacteria, and evolution, as is often the case, has reused prokaryotic processes and principles in eukaryotes.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a conclusion about evolutionary conservation of mechanical principles.

claim: Biofilms represent an intriguing and highly tractable model system to investigate the general role of mechanical forces in morphogenesis.
source: In summary, biofilms represent an intriguing and highly tractable model system to investigate the general role of mechanical forces in morphogenesis, and they provide a convenient system for morpho-engineering.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a conclusion about the utility of biofilms as a model system.

claim: Growth occurs primarily at the edge of the biofilm because of nutrient limitation at the center of the biofilm.
source: Soon after the initial expansion of the biofilm, growth occurs primarily at the edge of the biofilm because of nutrient limitation at the center of the biofilm (Liu et al., 2015; Yan et al., 2017; and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations and experimental data.

claim: At the biofilm center, cell death has been shown to drive pattern formation.
source: At the biofilm center, cell death has been shown to drive pattern formation (Asally et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The Poisson ratio ν of the biofilm is approximately 0.495, close to the incompressible limit.
source: From these data, we could calculate the Poisson's ratio ν = (3K – 2G') / 2(3K + G') ≈ 0.495, close to the incompressible limit (ν = 0.5).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on experimental measurements and calculations.

claim: The bulk modulus K of the biofilm is approximately 130 kPa, much larger than the shear modulus G'.
source: Using the relationship between normal force and shaft displacement, we calculated the bulk modulus K of the biofilm to be ~ 130 kPa; much larger than the shear modulus G'.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on experimental measurements.

claim: The residual layer contains primarily matrix material with few live cells.
source: After biofilm peeling, a weak signal can be observed in the WGA channel but not in the mKate2 channel, suggesting that the residual layer contains primarily extracellular polysaccharide but not live cells.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by fluorescence imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The normalized CFU in the residual layer is significantly lower than in the biofilm layer.
source: Normalized CFU (colony forming units) in the biofilm and the residual layers for 2-day-old biofilms grown on a 0.6% agar substrate. Paired t-tests (n = 4) were performed for statistical analyses. ** denotes p-value < 0.01.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: India ink is excluded from the biofilm and residual layer when the key matrix polysaccharide is present but not when it is absent.
source: India ink is excluded from the biofilm and residual layer when the key matrix polysaccharide is present (WT residual layer, WT biofilm, ΔABC biofilm) but not when the key matrix polysaccharide is absent (ΔvpsL biofilm).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by India ink staining experiments in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The final thickness of the biofilm layer is set by the availability of oxygen, which can generally penetrate into a biofilm to a distance of tens of microns.
source: Thus, we hypothesize that the final thickness of the biofilm layer is set by the availability of oxygen, which can generally penetrate into a biofilm to a distance of tens of microns (Okegbe et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a hypothesis and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The corrected biofilm thickness hf changes minimally with changing agar concentrations.
source: hf changes minimally with changing agar concentrations.

claim: The wrinkling and delamination instabilities occur within a 2-hr window.
source: The wrinkling and delamination instabilities occur within a 2-hr window.

claim: No localized cell death was observed to precede the formation of wrinkles or blisters at the biofilm periphery.
source: No localized cell death was observed to precede the formation of wrinkles or blisters.

claim: The wavelength of the patterns is independent of biofilm growth geometry (circle versus line).
source: Comparison of the wavelengths of the patterns for biofilms grown on identical agar substrates (0.5% agar) but in different initial geometries (circle (white) versus line (gray)). Unpaired t-tests with Welch's correction were performed for statistical analyses. p-value = 0.394. NS denotes not significant.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by statistical analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The characteristic length of the pattern inside the nutrient-limited zones differs from that of the morphological pattern outside of the zones.
source: We note that the characteristic length of the pattern inside the nutrient-limited zones (outlined with the red dotted circles in panels (B) and (C), images on the right), differs from that of the morphological pattern outside of the zones because the morphology inside the biofilm core has been shown to arise from localized cell death (Asally et al., 2012; Yan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to previous work.
